id_and_class.summary: Nick Bostrom holds that consciousness depends on computation, not on the material that performs it, so minds could run on substrates other than biological neurons. He develops this less as a theory of what consciousness is than as a premise for his simulation argument, anthropic reasoning, and the ethics of artificial minds.

conceptual_ground.explanatory_identity_claim: Consciousness is a product of the right computational processes. Mental states are defined by their functional roles, what they do, rather than what they are made of.
conceptual_ground.mind_body_relationship: Multiple realizability. Bostrom writes that if human minds can be simulated and simulated minds can be conscious, our own consciousness might be realized in a substrate other than biological neurons.
conceptual_ground.ontological_commitments: Computational processes and whatever physical substrate implements them, biological or artificial.
conceptual_ground.epistemic_access: Through computational neuroscience and philosophical reasoning about observers, probability, and simulation.

mechanism_and_dynamics.scope_of_consciousness: Phenomenal (as morally significant); Degrees of consciousness; Observer status
mechanism_and_dynamics.distinctive_mechanism_or_principle: Substrate independence: the same computation produces the same mental states whatever hardware runs it.
mechanism_and_dynamics.location_and_distribution: Wherever the relevant computation runs, in brains, computers, or a simulated world.
mechanism_and_dynamics.causation_and_functional_role: Being conscious shapes reasoning. Observer selection effects constrain what a conscious observer should believe about the universe, including whether it lives in a simulation.
core_claims_and_evidence: If minds can be simulated and simulated minds can be conscious, consciousness does not require biological neurons.
The simulation argument is coherent only if consciousness is computational, which makes computationalism a precondition of it.
Bostrom writes that an entity’s moral status depends at least in part on whether it is conscious and to what degree, implying consciousness comes in degrees.
Bostrom does not claim we live in a simulation; his computationalism rests on other grounds, including computational neuroscience.
mechanism_and_dynamics.basis_of_belief_or_evidence_type: Philosophical and probabilistic argument, informed by computational neuroscience.

empirics_and_critiques.criticisms_and_tensions: Bostrom assumes computational functionalism more than he argues for it, and he does not explain why computation should produce experience.
empirics_and_critiques.open_questions_and_limitations: Whether artificial minds can be conscious, and whether they should have rights, are questions the view raises but does not settle. Bostrom’s account is more epistemological than metaphysical.
empirics_and_critiques.ontological_coherence: Consistent with mainstream functionalism and with his work on simulation, existential risk, and whole brain emulation.

AI_consciousness.rationale: If consciousness is substrate-independent computation, artificial systems running the right processes would be conscious, and Bostrom ties their moral status to it.

survival_beyond_death.rationale: Biological death ends consciousness unless its computation is reproduced elsewhere; if we are simulated, what happens to us depends on the simulators.

meaning_and_purpose.rationale: If our world is a simulation built by an advanced civilization, it may have a purpose set by its makers, but Bostrom does not claim to know.

virtual_immortality.rationale: Substrate independence implies that a simulated mind could continue a person’s consciousness, in line with Bostrom’s interest in whole brain emulation.

sources_and_references.title_with_names: Bostrom’s Computational Functionalism (Landscape of Consciousness), Nick Bostrom
